# Book I, Proposition 18

*The greater side subtends the greater angle*

> In any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/18-idea.svg" alt="The longer side (red) always faces the bigger angle (red), and the shorter side (blue) faces the smaller angle (blue)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>The longer side (red) always faces the bigger angle (red), and the shorter side (blue) faces the smaller angle (blue).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/18.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.18, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let ABC be a triangle having the side AC greater than AB;

I say that the angle ABC is also greater than the angle BCA.

For, since AC is greater than AB, let AD be made equal to AB [I. 3], and let BD be joined.

Then, since the angle ADB is an exterior angle of the triangle BCD,

it is greater than the interior and opposite angle DCB. [I. 16]

But the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD,

since the side AB is equal to AD;

therefore the angle ABD is also greater than the angle ACB;

therefore the angle ABC is much greater than the angle ACB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop18.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop18.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- In any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle. -/
theorem Prop18 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖) :
    ∠ B C A < ∠ A B C := by
  -- For let ABC be a triangle having the side AC greater than AB;
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hB_C : B ≠ C := hABC.ne₂₃
  have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hA_C
  have hB_AC : ¬ OnLine B AC := hABC.acb.off_line hA_AC hC_AC
  -- I say that the angle ABC is also greater than the angle BCA.
  -- For, since AC is greater than AB, let AD be made equal to AB [I. 3], and let BD be joined.
  /- I.3 cuts off from AC, beginning at A, a straight line AD equal to AB; D lies
     between A and C. Joining BD is Postulate 1; Lean needs only the points. -/
  obtain ⟨D, hADC, hAD_AB⟩ := Prop3 hA_B h
  have hD_AC : OnLine D AC := on_line_of_between_ends hADC hA_AC hC_AC
  have hD_C : D ≠ C := (ne_of_between (between_symm hADC)).symm
  have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADC
  -- Then, since the angle ADB is an exterior angle of the triangle BCD,
  /- BCD is a triangle, since B is off the straight line AC on which C and D lie;
     and its side CD is produced to A, since D lies between C and A. -/
  have hBCD : Triangle B C D := (Triangle.of_line hC_AC hD_AC hD_C.symm hB_AC).cab
  have hCDA : Between C D A := between_symm hADC
  -- it is greater than the interior and opposite angle DCB. [I. 16]
  have hDCB_BDA : ∠ D C B < ∠ B D A := (Prop16 hBCD hCDA).1
  /- I.16 names the exterior angle BDA; read from the other arm, it is ADB. -/
  have hB_D : B ≠ D := fun e => hB_AC (e ▸ hD_AC)
  have hDCB_ADB : ∠ D C B < ∠ A D B := by
    rw [angle_symm hB_D hA_D] at hDCB_BDA
    exact hDCB_BDA
  -- But the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD,
  -- since the side AB is equal to AD;
  /- This is I.5, for the isosceles triangle ABD. As stated, I.5 also speaks of the
     angles under the base, so it asks for AB and AD produced; any points beyond B
     and D will do (`Prop5.base`). -/
  have hABD : Triangle A B D := (Triangle.of_line hA_AC hD_AC hA_D hB_AC).acb
  have hAB_AD : ‖A B‖ = ‖A D‖ := hAD_AB.symm
  have hABD_ADB : ∠ A B D = ∠ A D B := Prop5.base hABD hAB_AD
  -- therefore the angle ABD is also greater than the angle ACB;
  /- The angle DCB is the angle ACB, since D lies on the ray from C through A. -/
  have hDCB_ACB : ∠ D C B = ∠ A C B := angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hCDA) hB_C
  have hACB_ABD : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B D := by
    rw [← hDCB_ACB, hABD_ADB]
    exact hDCB_ADB
  -- therefore the angle ABC is much greater than the angle ACB.
  /- Much greater, because the angle ABD is only a part of the angle ABC: since D
     lies between A and C, BD falls within the angle ABC, which is made up of the
     angles ABD and DBC (`angle_add_of_between`); the angle DBC, an angle of the
     triangle DBC, is something (`Triangle.angle_pos`); and the whole is greater
     than the part [C.N. 5]. -/
  have hABD_ABC : ∠ A B D < ∠ A B C := by
    rw [angle_add_of_between hABC.acb hADC]
    exact CommonNotion5 hBCD.cab.angle_pos
  have hACB_ABC : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B C := lt_trans hACB_ABD hABD_ABC
  -- Therefore etc.
  /- The angle ACB is the angle BCA, named from the other arm. -/
  rw [angle_symm hB_C hA_C]
  exact hACB_ABC
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**Which comes first.** I.18 and I.19 say almost the same words in a different order, and Heath gives a rule for telling them apart: "the *datum* comes first and the *quaesitum* second, the *datum* being in this proposition the greater *side* and in the next the greater *angle*" (vol. 1, p. 283). He passes on Isaac Todhunter's memory aid as well: "In order to assist the student in remembering which of these two propositions [I. 18, 19] is demonstrated directly and which indirectly, it may be observed that the order is similar to that in I. 5 and I. 6" (vol. 1, p. 283). I.18, like I.5, goes straight at its conclusion; I.19, like I.6, gets there by *reductio*.

**A citation Euclid leaves out.** Euclid brackets I.3 and I.16, but "the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD, since the side AB is equal to AD" is I.5, given without a reference. Lean has to cite it, for the isosceles triangle ABD. Our I.5 also speaks of the angles under the base, so `Prop5.base` produces AB and AD for it (Post. 2), and only the first half is used. The exterior angle itself needs no producing: I.3 has put D between A and C, so the side CD of the triangle BCD is already produced, to A.

**"Much greater."** The angle DCB that I.16 gives is the triangle's angle ACB, because D lies on the ray from C through A (`OnRay.of_between`, `angle_onRay_left`). And "much greater" needs BD within the angle ABC, so that ABD is a part of it: since D lies between A and C, the angle ABC is made up of ABD and DBC (`angle_add_of_between`), and DBC is something, B being off AC (`Triangle.angle_pos`). Then come Common Notion 5, the whole greater than the part, and `lt_trans`: what is greater than the greater is greater still.

**The modern way.** Name the sides a = BC, b = CA, c = AB. The law of cosines gives cos C − cos B = (b − c)(b + c − a)(a + b + c)/(2abc), and b + c is greater than a (that is I.20), so when b is greater than c, cos B is less than cos C and the angle B is the greater.
